fact_sheet.business_description: First Republic Bank provides relationship banking, residential lending, and wealth management services to affluent households [D01]. The institution operates as a deposit-funded bank currently navigating a significant liquidity stabilization process [D01, D04].
segments_and_separable_assets: Wealth Management: provides fee income but lacks loss-absorbing capital for the balance sheet [D06].
Residential Lending: primary asset base; recovery value depends on loan realizations after senior claims [D01, D05].
Deposit Franchise: value dependent on customer relationship survival and retention [D01].
economics_vs_peers: FY2022 ROE 11.60% and CET1 9.17% [D06]. Margin gap and direct comparison vs JPMorgan (14% ROE / 13.2% CET1) and Bank of America are hindered by different business mixes and recent funding instability [D06]. Deposit growth was 12.9% in 2022, but Q4 2022 NIM fell to 2.45% from 2.71% in Q3 [D02, D03].
capital_structure: Includes $30bn in uninsured term deposits (initial 120-day term) provided by a banking consortium [D03, D04]. Year-end 2022 borrowings were $15.279bn with cash of $4.283bn [D02]. March 10-15 Fed borrowing range was $20-109bn [D03]. Common equity is junior to depositors, secured creditors, and preferred holders [D05].
price_and_valuation: Price: $34.27 (March 16 close) [D04]. Market cap: ~$6.38bn [D04]. P/E: 4.15x [D04]. P/TBV: 0.462x [D04]. Dividend: Suspended post-cutoff [D03, D04].
Valuation is highly sensitive to fair-value stress on assets and replacement funding costs; historical multiples (e.g., P/B) are not reliable without current marks [D04, D05].
management_board_governance: Management and board are currently managing the stabilization process in coordination with regulators and an eleven-bank consortium [D01, D03]. No specific information provided on staggered boards, pill, or prior activist history [not in pack].
shareholder_base_and_liquidity: 186.219m shares outstanding [D04]. Short interest, index ownership, and average daily volume [not in pack].
event_or_catalyst_evidence: Stabilization of deposit base via $30bn consortium placement [D01, D03]. Potential for asset sale or further regulatory resolution [D05]. Suspension of common dividend [D03].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Liquidity assistance protects depositors but exposes common equity to asset marks and expensive replacement funding [D03, D05].
Risk of forced asset sale or regulatory intervention transferring franchise value away from common shareholders [D05].
Lack of current deposit retention data [D02, D03].

gate1.edge_statement: Third Point lacks a structural edge in this liquidity event because the valuation is highly sensitive to unknown fair-value marks and the common equity sits behind layers of priority capital with no governance control.
gate1.one_line_verdict: A banking franchise in a liquidity-driven stabilization process where the common equity is effectively a subordinated call option with no floor.

gate2.variant_view: The market prices First Republic as a viable franchise undergoing standard liquidity stabilization, failing to account for the catastrophic impairment of common equity under fair-value stress and high-cost replacement funding. We believe the common equity is effectively a subordinated call option with no floor, as any regulatory resolution or asset sale will likely prioritize senior claims and leave little to no residual value for shareholders [D04, D05].

final.memo:
First Republic Bank is a relationship-based financial institution currently navigating a severe liquidity crisis that has rendered the common equity a highly speculative and likely worthless instrument [D01, D04]. While the market may view the $30 billion consortium deposit placement as a lifeline, we view it as a bridge that fails to address the underlying asset-liability mismatch [D03, D04].

When we assess the post-event earnings power of the remaining franchise, it is clear that the common equity sits behind senior depositors, secured creditors, and preferred holders [D05]. With valuation highly sensitive to unknown fair-value marks on the residential loan portfolio, the theoretical book value is decoupled from reality [D04, D05].

Market participants are attempting to price a viable going concern, but they fail to account for the catastrophic impairment of common equity under stress and the prohibitively high cost of replacement funding [D04, D05]. The dividend suspension is a tacit admission of the capital pressures the bank faces [D03, D04].

The current plan is managed entirely by an eleven-bank consortium and regulatory authorities, leaving common shareholders with no governance levers to protect their interests [D01, D03]. Because we identify no constructive role for an activist and no path to influence management or regulators, there is no viable route for us to participate [D01, D03].

The risks here are binary: a regulatory seizure or forced asset sale would likely result in total equity impairment [D03, D05]. Given the absence of a hard floor and the lack of a clear governance path to extract value, we see no investment opportunity here.

We have determined that this situation is a pass. We will not be participating in the equity, and we find the risk profile incompatible with our mandate.
